0.0.n: This adjective comes directly before 店 to describe it.

0.1.n: The noun is followed by を because it is what the speaker found.

0.2.n: を marks 店 as the thing the speaker found.

0.3.n: The polite past form of 見つける reports a completed discovery.

1.0.n: ガチャポン refers to capsule toys sold through vending machines.

1.1.n: の links ガチャポン to 店, telling us what kind of shop it is.

1.2.n: Here, 店 is described by the noun before の.

1.3.n: です politely ends the sentence; what it refers to is understood from context.

2.0.n: Usually an adjective, すごい stands alone here as an excited reaction.

2.2.n: 全部 refers to everything in view, with the rest of the thought left unfinished.

3.0.n: こっち is a casual way to point out a nearby direction or area.

3.1.n: も adds this area to the one already mentioned.

3.2.n: 全部 emphasizes that everything on this side is included as well.

4.0.n: ハッピーターン is the name of a Japanese rice cracker snack brand.

4.1.n: ある says something is present or available; casual speech often drops が before it.

0.tip: Japanese often leaves out the subject when context makes it clear who did the action.

1.tip: A noun followed by の can describe another noun, as in ガチャポンの店.

2.tip: The unfinished phrase conveys surprise without spelling out a complete thought.

3.lit: This side too, all of it!
3.tip: も means this side shares what was just noticed about the other side.

4.tip: ある can express availability, so this naturally means they have Happy Turn here.
